question: In the Li3PO4-coated NCM study, how much did the charge-transfer resistance rise over 50 cycles for the bare and the coated material, and what capacity did each retain after 100 cycles at 1C?

trace.query: SELECT id, page, text, strength FROM atoms WHERE lower(text) LIKE '%li3po4%' OR lower(text) LIKE '%li3po%' OR lower(text) LIKE '%charge-transfer%' OR lower(text) LIKE '%charge transfer%' OR lower(text) LIKE '%resistance%' ORDER BY page, id
SELECT id, page, text FROM lines WHERE page IN (8) ORDER BY page, line_no

WITH b AS (SELECT text AS t FROM lines WHERE id='p8.L38'), c AS (SELECT text AS t FROM lines WHERE id='p8.L40')
SELECT ROUND(CAST(regexp_extract(b.t,' to ([0-9.]+)',1) AS DOUBLE) - CAST(regexp_extract(b.t,'from ([0-9.]+) to',1) AS DOUBLE), 2) AS bare_rise,
ROUND(CAST(regexp_extract(c.t,' to ([0-9.]+)',1) AS DOUBLE) - CAST(regexp_extract(c.t,'from ([0-9.]+) to',1) AS DOUBLE), 2) AS coated_rise
FROM b, c

rendered: The study is the Li3PO4 (LPO)-modified NCM work. Over 50[1] cycles, the charge-transfer resistance of the bare NCM rose from 27.99[2] to 224.04[3] Ω, an increase of 196.05[4] Ω. For the LPO-coated NCM it rose from 14.88[5] to 144.75[6] Ω, an increase of 129.87[7] Ω, so the coated material's resistance growth was smaller. After 100[8] cycles at 1C[9], the bare NCM retained 75.4%[10] of its initial discharge capacity, and the LPO-coated NCM retained 88.4%[11] of its capacity.
